summary:
Île-de-France stands under the French national framework: France's rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage apply uniformly across the region, and no separate regional regime governs transgender visitors.

Paris and its suburbs carry a disproportionate share of France's recorded anti-LGBT+ offending. The Interior Ministry's statistics service recorded 4,800 anti-LGBT+ offences nationwide in 2024, up 5% on 2023, with crimes and délicts rising 14% per year since 2016; only about 4% of victims file complaints. Acts concentrate in urban units above 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris, whose recorded rate of 22 per 100,000 residents stands against a national rate of 7. The ministry note attributes part of that gap to non-resident victims and commuters, and records that more than 70% of recorded victims are men.

Large LGBT events in the Paris agglomeration now draw far-right counter-presence and a heavy security response. Paris Pride on 28 June 2025 was classed a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry, with CRS police reinforcements deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march; police were framed as separating the opposing groups.

Paris holds France's densest LGBTQ infrastructure. As of 2004 the city counted 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops, hosts France's only officially organised gaybourneys, and stages the annual Paris Pride parade. The city also carries a documented targeted-violence history: Bertrand Delanoë, France's first openly gay mayor of Paris, elected in 2002, was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals.
tangentialFactors:
The Interior Ministry's Infraction rapide n°53 of May 2025 notes that Paris's elevated recorded rate partly reflects non-resident victims and commuters passing through the region, so the raw figure overstates risk to residents while still indicating volume at places a visitor would use.

Recorded victims are more than 70% men, and only about 4% of victims file complaints nationally, so official counts understate incidence across all of France including the region.
localsOnly:
Residents of Île-de-France live under the same national legal baseline as visitors: same-sex civil partnerships (PACS) since 1999, same-sex marriage since 2013, anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation since 1985 and gender identity since 2012, legal gender change without surgery or medical diagnosis since 2017, and declassification of gender dysphoria as a mental illness dating from 2010.

Local exposure concentrates in the recorded-offence pattern: the Paris urban unit's rate of 22 anti-LGBT+ offences per 100,000 against a national 7, with national complaint-filing at roughly 4% of victims.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Infraction rapide n°53 figures are national, with the Paris urban unit singled out; Île-de-France as a whole is not broken out separately, so the region's own rate beyond Paris is unresolved in the sources.

The 140-venue count for Paris dates from 2004 and is not updated in the source; current venue density is not sourced here.

No region-specific signal on detention placement, border-document checks or facilities access was identified in this inventory; those layers sit with the national record.
